courses.name: Personal & Professional Development

content.description2: This course is a first-year requirement and aims to stimulate personal development, namely, being able to actively, consciously and ethically orientate oneself in relation to others and the world. It supports the development of core personal and academic skills that enhance critical thinking and independent learning. It seeks to improve and develop academic writing and presenting skills and helps students develop the foundational skills and attitudes to reflect on societal issues and engage with societal partners.
content.profile: Develops academic writing and research-literacy skills alongside personal development and civic engagement. Students locate and evaluate scholarly sources, synthesize literature, formulate research questions and arguments, and construct a research-paper introduction. A community-engaged project with a societal partner connects these skills to collaboration, reflection and practical contribution. Personal development planning addresses learning goals, self-efficacy, and stress and time management; the course also considers responsible academic use of AI.

content.topics: Scholarly sources and research questions; Argumentation and thesis statements; Literature synthesis; Academic integrity and referencing; Community engagement; Personal learning goals and reflective learning; Collaborative learning; Self-efficacy; Stress and time management; Responsible use of AI
content.methods: Scholarly literature searching and source evaluation; Literature synthesis; CARS model for research introductions; Reflective development planning; Community project co-design

courses.name: Consumer Product Design

content.description2: You will learn how to function in a ‘real-world’ design and development team for consumer products. We go through the phases of design and development: probe customer needs, translate these into a product concept, develop a fabrication method, analyze sustainability, analyze costs and proceeds. Design and development involves interviewing customers, brainstorming, laboratory experiments, quantitative modeling, constructing a prototype, and considering protection of intellectual property.
content.profile: Teaches consumer-product design and development through projects that progress from understanding an existing product to creating a new one. Students investigate product mechanisms and environmental impact, interview potential customers, translate needs into specifications, select concepts, and develop production plans and prototypes where feasible. The final project integrates these stages with industrial scaling and elementary economic analysis. Sustainability, including material use, repairability, lifespan and circularity, informs design decisions throughout.
content.discipline: Product design; Product and process development; Sustainable design
content.topics: Consumer needs; Product concepts and specifications; Product working mechanisms; Prototyping; Laboratory-to-industrial production scaling; Materials and resource use; Product lifespan, repairability and circularity; Environmental impact; Production costs and commercial viability
content.methods: Consumer interviews; Needs ranking and specification development; Concept-criteria matrices; Quantitative product modelling; Product investigation and experimentation; Prototyping; Process-flow diagrams and material balances; Environmental-impact estimation; Break-even analysis

courses.contribution: Actual consumer-needs interviews, specifications, concept choice, quantitative product models, prototypes/fabrication and circularity/cost analysis. Complementary user-oriented physical-product methods, not a guaranteed software interface or HCI project.

courses.name: Research Methods & Statistics

content.description2: Research Methods & Statistics gives you a strong foundation in how business management—and social and behavioral sciences—move from mere practices to true fields of scientific study. You’ll learn how to plan research logically, from designing studies to working with real data using experimental and survey techniques. You’ll also study descriptive and inferential statistics, with a brief intro to multivariate tools.
content.profile: Introduces empirical research design and statistical analysis, followed by a substantial student research project. Students study operationalization, measurement quality, sampling, surveys and experimental and nonexperimental designs, then descriptive statistics, estimation, hypothesis testing and introductory regression. R and R Commander support data display and analysis. Project teams develop instruments and a research plan, collect and analyze data, and report results under explicit research-ethics and privacy requirements.

content.topics: Scientific inquiry and hypotheses; Operationalization and measurement; Reliability and validity; Survey construction and sampling; Randomized and quasi-experimental designs; Nonexperimental and qualitative research; Descriptive statistics; Sampling distributions and estimation; Hypothesis testing and confidence intervals; Association and regression; Research ethics and anonymous data collection
content.methods: Survey design; Probability and nonprobability sampling; Experimental and nonexperimental research design; R and R Commander data analysis; Descriptive statistics and visualization; Scale-reliability analysis; One- and two-sample mean tests; ANOVA; Chi-square tests; Correlation and regression; Empirical data collection and analysis

courses.contribution: Empirical research design, sampling/surveys/experiments and R-based inference/regression in a real research project. Complementary scientific evaluation methods; no computing dataset or independent computer-science thesis guaranteed.

courses.name: AI Ethics

courses.name: Decision-making in AI

content.description2: Introduces planning techniques for AI systems in deterministic and non‑deterministic environments. Addresses uncertainty, partial observability, resource planning and optimizing behaviour under constraints.
content.profile: Develops the mathematical foundations of intelligent-agent decisions under uncertainty. Probability and Bayesian networks support belief updating and inference, while temporal models address changing environments. Decision theory, Markov decision processes, partial observability and bandit problems connect uncertainty to policies and expected utility. Multi-agent decisions introduce strategic and collective interaction, and probabilistic programming provides a framework for expressing models. Students work through equations, numerical examples and scientific papers.

content.methods: Probabilistic inference; Bayesian-network modelling; Temporal probabilistic modelling; Expected-utility analysis; Sequential decision modelling; Game-theoretic analysis; Probabilistic programming

HCBCOGN212.name: Perception & Action
HCBCOGN212.description2: Explores neural mechanisms behind perception and action. Examines how the brain processes sensory information and guides goal‑directed behaviour using methods from cognitive neuroscience and neuropsychology.

HCBPSYC111.name: Social Psychology
HCBPSYC111.description2: Covers main theories, findings and principles of social psychology, emphasising its scientific approach to understanding how people’s feelings, thoughts and behaviour are influenced by the presence of others.
HCBPSYC111.profile: Introduces the scientific study of how thoughts, feelings and behaviour are shaped by other people and social situations. Social cognition, the self, influence and persuasion lead into group processes, prejudice, aggression, prosocial behaviour, attraction and close relationships. Students critically examine empirical research, synthesize findings from journal articles, formulate theory-guided questions and design a feasible study. The final project proposes research rather than conducting an empirical investigation.
HCBPSYC111.topics: Social cognition and person perception; The self and self-motives; Social influence; Persuasion, attitudes and behaviour; Group processes; Prejudice, stereotyping and discrimination; Prejudice reduction; Interpersonal aggression; Prosocial behaviour; Interpersonal attraction and close relationships
HCBPSYC111.methods: Critical appraisal of empirical social-psychology research; Literature synthesis; Theory-guided hypothesis formulation; Research design for a proposed social-psychology study

DISDATA312.name: Robotics
DISDATA312.description2: Covers computational problems in robotics. Includes forward and inverse kinematics, motion planning, collision avoidance and robotic grasping and manipulation.
DISDATA312.profile: Studies computational problems in robot motion and manipulation, supported by linear algebra, calculus and geometric modelling. Students analyze forward and inverse kinematics, configuration spaces, collision-free motion planning and grasping, with shorter introductions to sensing and control. Practical work programs a robot arm and gripper; research investigates inverse kinematics for an articulated structure. A smaller component examines a chosen legal, ethical, safety or human-robot issue.
DISDATA312.topics: Robot architecture and industrial automation; Rotations, orientations and rigid transformations; Forward and inverse kinematics; Trajectory generation; Configuration spaces and obstacles; Exact, approximate and sampling-based motion planning; Collision detection; Sensing and control; Form and force closure; Caging; Non-prehensile manipulation; Social and ethical aspects of robotics
DISDATA312.methods: Coordinate-frame modelling of articulated structures; Analytic and iterative inverse kinematics; Mathematica computation; Configuration-space modelling; Motion-planning analysis; Collision-detection analysis; Instantaneous-motion and wrench analysis; Robot-arm and gripper programming; Modelling of physical manipulation

BENENTR111.name: Consumer Product Design
BENENTR111.description2: You will learn how to function in a ‘real-world’ design and development team for consumer products. We go through the phases of design and development: probe customer needs, translate these into a product concept, develop a fabrication method, analyze sustainability, analyze costs and proceeds. Design and development involves interviewing customers, brainstorming, laboratory experiments, quantitative modeling, constructing a prototype, and considering protection of intellectual property.
BENENTR111.profile: Teaches consumer-product design and development through projects that progress from understanding an existing product to creating a new one. Students investigate product mechanisms and environmental impact, interview potential customers, translate needs into specifications, select concepts, and develop production plans and prototypes where feasible. The final project integrates these stages with industrial scaling and elementary economic analysis. Sustainability, including material use, repairability, lifespan and circularity, informs design decisions throughout.
BENENTR111.topics: Consumer needs; Product concepts and specifications; Product working mechanisms; Prototyping; Laboratory-to-industrial production scaling; Materials and resource use; Product lifespan, repairability and circularity; Environmental impact; Production costs and commercial viability
BENENTR111.methods: Consumer interviews; Needs ranking and specification development; Concept-criteria matrices; Quantitative product modelling; Product investigation and experimentation; Prototyping; Process-flow diagrams and material balances; Environmental-impact estimation; Break-even analysis

DISARIN111.name: AI Ethics
DISARIN111.description2: Explores philosophical foundations and implications of AI. Examines the history of AI, ethical issues like interpretability, bias and alignment, debates about AI consciousness and implications for human nature.
DISARIN111.profile: Examines AI through ethical theory and psychological accounts of human behaviour and interaction. Ethical debates address fairness, privacy, responsibility, alignment, moral status and political or existential risks. Psychological perspectives consider development, clinical care, social and organizational relationships, forensic applications and cognitive neuroscience. Students synthesize literature and apply ethical frameworks in an analytical psychology project and a research-grounded podcast, with a creative communication component.
DISARIN111.topics: Algorithmic fairness and bias; Privacy and surveillance; Responsibility and accountability; Human-value alignment; Moral status of AI; Existential risk and democratic implications; Trust and agency in human-AI interaction; AI in clinical care; Child development and AI; Social and organizational effects of AI; AI in forensic psychology; Cognitive and socioemotional development; AI consciousness and sentience
DISARIN111.methods: Ethical-framework application; Philosophical argument evaluation; Psychological-literature synthesis; Theory-based analysis of AI applications; Research podcast scripting, recording and editing
